name: Fairness can soften unfair rules
description: Foundational claim drawn from Roman jurisprudence that aequitas—fairness and proportion—guides judges and lawmakers in tempering rigid rules so outcomes align with justice in concrete cases.
plainSummary: Sometimes applying a rule word-for-word produces an unfair outcome. Many frameworks hold that judges and lawmakers may soften rigid rules so concrete cases align better with justice.
whyRoot: Rules are written in advance for typical cases; life produces outliers. Without a safety valve for proportion and fairness, law becomes mechanical cruelty. Equity is a root because justice is not the same as a checklist.

name: Bodily self-determination for competent adults
description: Foundational claim that competent adults have primary moral and legal authority over their own bodies, including medical choices, absent overriding harm to others.
plainSummary: Competent adults should generally direct decisions about their own bodies, including medical choices, unless a strong overriding reason exists—such as serious harm to others.
whyRoot: The body is the medium through which a person experiences the world; if others controlled it by default, personal agency would mean little. Bodily authority is treated as a root because it pairs moral personhood with a zone of decision-making that others must justify crossing.

name: Christian scripture and tradition as moral authority
description: Foundational claim, for faith-based branches of the graph, that Christian scripture and ecclesial tradition (especially in Catholic and Orthodox moral theology) authoritatively frame the classification of serious moral failure, including the tradition of capital vices (deadly sins).
plainSummary: Within Catholic and broader Christian moral theology, sacred scripture and the Church's teaching office (where accepted) supply norms for virtue, vice, and conscience.
whyRoot: For frameworks that take this stance, lists like the capital vices are not mere opinion: they classify recurring ways human willing goes wrong. The graph stops here for believers; others can still read the downstream principles as historically influential moral categories.

name: Coherent legal order
description: Foundational civilian ideal that legal rules should form a coherent body, developed through reasoned commentary and (where appropriate) codification, traceable to Roman models of ordered private law and public authority.
plainSummary: The framework holds that legal rules should fit together into a clear, coherent system—often worked out through careful reasoning and codes—rather than a messy pile of unrelated edicts.
whyRoot: People need to know what duties and rights they actually have. If law is a tangle of contradictions, planning and fairness collapse. Coherence is treated as foundational because predictable, unified rules are what let strangers coordinate without constant conflict.

name: Equal moral consideration
description: Foundational claim that all persons (or all in a defined scope) deserve equal standing in moral and often legal reasoning about rights, burdens, and opportunities, absent specific differences that justify unequal treatment.
plainSummary: The framework holds that everyone who counts in the discussion should matter equally when weighing rights, burdens, and opportunities, unless a specific reason supports different treatment.
whyRoot: Arbitrary favoritism turns law into club rules. Starting from equal consideration forces reasons for unequal treatment into the open. It is a root because it blocks treating 'my group counts more' as a silent default.

name: Evidence anchors high-stakes law and policy
description: Foundational commitment that when laws or regulations materially affect health, safety, or liberty, they should align with credible empirical and expert consensus where such evidence exists.
plainSummary: When laws or rules seriously affect health, safety, or freedom, they should align with the best available evidence and expert consensus when that exists.
whyRoot: When mistakes are costly and hard to reverse, guessing is a poor basis for coercion. Anchoring high-stakes rules to the best shared picture of facts is a root commitment: it reduces arbitrary harm and makes public justification possible.

name: Parties owe each other fair dealing
description: Foundational commitment to reciprocal fairness in performance and enforcement: parties may not weaponize formal rights to surprise, oppress, or take advantage in ways civil-law and common-law systems often capture under abuse-of-right or good-faith doctrines.
plainSummary: In bargains and ongoing legal relationships, the framework expects each side to treat the other fairly—not only to follow the letter of the contract while acting in a one-sided or exploitative way.
whyRoot: Bargaining assumes each party can count on something beyond gamesmanship. If only the bare form of words counted, clever abuse would win and cooperation would stay fragile. Fair dealing is a root commitment because it names the minimum mutual respect that makes long-term relationships workable.

name: Fidelity to the spirit of agreements
description: Foundational commitment to loyalty to the bargain (allied with pacta-related ideas in many traditions): performance and interpretation should respect the agreement's intent and the trust the other party reasonably placed in the undertaking.
plainSummary: Once someone undertakes a commitment, the framework holds that they should stand by its purpose and reasonable expectations—not only the narrowest reading that benefits them.
whyRoot: Promises coordinate expectations over time. If people could always dodge the point of a deal whenever a loophole appeared, others could not rely on undertakings, and cooperation would stall. Fidelity to the bargain is foundational because it is what makes words actually binding in practice.

name: Truthfulness in agreements and dealings
description: Foundational commitment that veracity and good-faith disclosure matter in forming, performing, and interpreting obligations; a building block for doctrines of fraud, misrepresentation, and implied duties in many legal systems.
plainSummary: In legal and private relationships, people should tell the truth, avoid misleading others, and disclose what fairness requires—not exploit silence or fine print in bad faith.
whyRoot: Voluntary cooperation rests on a shared picture of reality: if people can lie or hide what matters, planning, exchange, and trust break down. Honesty is treated as a stopping point because without it, weaker parties are easy to manipulate and almost nothing else in private law can be relied on.

name: Liberty as default; limits require justification
description: Foundational liberal or libertarian commitment that interference with voluntary choice requires a positive justification (harm prevention, consent of the governed, etc.), rather than the reverse.
plainSummary: The framework holds that people should generally be free to choose for themselves. Restricting freedom calls for a substantive reason—such as preventing harm—rather than habit or preference alone.
whyRoot: Liberty is costly to restrict and easy to abuse: every constraint needs a public justification. This root flips the burden so freedom is presumed and interference must earn its place—so power cannot treat restriction as the default posture of government.

name: Human life as intrinsically significant
description: Foundational claim that human life is valuable in itself, often used as a root for autonomy and medical ethics arguments within many frameworks.
plainSummary: Human life matters for its own sake—not only because it is useful. Many arguments about ethics and medicine start from this idea.
whyRoot: If life only mattered when it was convenient or productive, people could be discarded whenever costs rose. Treating human life as carrying weight on its own is a stopping point for a huge swath of medical and legal reasoning: it says persons are not mere instruments.

name: Reduce suffering
description: Classical utilitarian starting point: moral weight attaches to the reduction of suffering (and often the promotion of well-being) across those affected.
plainSummary: Morally, reducing pain and hardship (and often improving well-being) for everyone affected by a decision carries weight.
whyRoot: Suffering is the clearest signal that something is going wrong for a subject of experience. Many ethical systems stop here because once suffering counts, there is reason to weigh outcomes and side effects instead of treating people as props in someone else's story.

name: Basic moral truths are open to human reason
description: Foundational claim associated with classical natural-law theory (including Thomism): core requirements of practical reason—such as prohibitions on grave injustice and certain disordered acts—are in principle accessible through reflection on human nature and the common good, not only through scripture.
plainSummary: In the Thomistic family of views, people can often know—without special revelation—that certain actions are wrong or disordered, because they bear on human flourishing and justice.
whyRoot: If some moral structure is knowable in principle, then religious and secular interlocutors can still argue about vices, virtues, and law on overlapping ground. This axiom does not deny revelation; it marks a distinct stopping point for what reason alone is said to reach.

name: Prior decisions bind or strongly guide later ones
description: Foundational commitment that adjudication should be stable and predictable by treating prior court decisions as authoritative or highly persuasive absent compelling reason to depart—core to the Anglo-American common law tradition.
plainSummary: Prior court decisions should usually bind or strongly guide later decisions, so the law stays predictable—unless a compelling reason supports changing course.
whyRoot: Legal disputes are supposed to be settled by rules people could have seen coming. If every case started from scratch, law would be arbitrary and investment in cooperation would shrink. Precedent is a root commitment to stability and notice.

name: Preventable death requires strong justification
description: Foundational commitment that deaths avoidable through known means (medical, policy, or infrastructure) ought not to occur without strong justification; common in public-health and longevity-oriented frameworks.
plainSummary: Frameworks that treat preventable death as unacceptable hold that when harm can be avoided through medicine, policy, or infrastructure, allowing it to occur requires a strong justification. That stance is common in public health and longevity-oriented worldviews.
whyRoot: When harm can be prevented at reasonable cost, letting it occur anyway normally requires a positive defense—otherwise neglect looks like a choice. This root ties the possibility of action to moral urgency rather than regret alone.

name: A written constitution is the highest law
description: Foundational commitment that political authority should be structured by a written charter that allocates powers, defines institutions, and stands above ordinary legislation—central to the U.S. federal order.
plainSummary: The framework holds that the basic rules of government belong in a written charter above ordinary laws: it divides power, sets up institutions, and limits what legislatures can do.
whyRoot: Power needs stable, public limits so people can plan their lives and hold rulers accountable. A supreme written charter is a root in this tradition because it makes those limits visible and harder to erase in a single ordinary vote.

name: Contempt, obstruction, and abuse of legal process
description: Legal constructs punishing disrespect or defiance toward courts and lawful authority, false statements to investigators, and manipulation of procedure—loosely analogous to moral concerns about hubris, defiance of legitimate order, and contempt for truth in institutional settings.

name: Criminal force and violence against the person
description: Legal constructs governing assault, battery, homicide, and related offenses—where the state punishes unjustified injury or credible threats, often discussed alongside moral critiques of wrath and disproportionate anger.

name: Fraud, theft, and wrongful appropriation
description: Legal constructs that prohibit acquiring or withholding another's property or entitlement through deception, stealth, or abuse of trust—often discussed alongside moral critiques of covetousness and envy.

name: Intoxication and substance-related offenses
description: Legal constructs addressing public drunkenness, driving under the influence, and controlled-substance rules—an imperfect but recurring legal analogue to moral warnings about intemperance and disordered appetite (including gluttony in its broader classical sense).

name: Negligence and breach of duty of care
description: Private-law constructs imposing liability when a person fails to meet a standard of care owed to others—one legal analogue (among others) to moral blame for culpable omission or sloth, though civil negligence does not require spiritual apathy.

name: Right to access experimental therapy
description: Legal concept covering circumstances under which patients may access therapies not yet fully approved under ordinary regulatory pathways.

name: Sexual offenses, consent, and privacy
description: Legal constructs addressing non-consensual sexual acts, exploitation of incapacity, and privacy-related sexual wrongs—areas where modern law foregrounds autonomy and harm, while historical and religious moral language often emphasized lust and chastity.

name: Bodily autonomy
description: Derived principle: persons have substantial authority over what happens to their own bodies, including medical decisions.

name: Good faith (bona fides) in private law
description: Synthesis principle from classical Roman jurisprudence: obligations, interpretation, and conduct in private law should be guided by bona fides—honesty, fair dealing, and loyalty to the bargain—rather than compliance with the letter alone.
plainSummary: Roman private law ties these ideas together: honesty, fair dealing, and faithfulness to agreements—so obligations and interpretation are guided by bona fides, not bare formalism alone.

name: Envy (invidia) as capital vice
description: Derived principle: invidia (envy) is the capital vice of sadness at another's excellence or happiness, distinct from righteous indignation at injustice; it tends toward detraction, schadenfreude, and hostility.
plainSummary: In this tradition, envy is sorrow or resentment at another's good—wishing to lower them or possess what is theirs in a disordered way.

name: Gluttony (gula) as capital vice
description: Derived principle: gula (gluttony) is the capital vice of intemperance in eating and drinking—classically including excessive concern for costly or refined fare, not merely caloric excess.
plainSummary: In this tradition, gluttony is not only eating too much: it is inordinate desire in the realm of food and drink—quantity, delicacy, or ritual that disorders health, sobriety, or solidarity.

name: Greed (avaritia) as capital vice
description: Derived principle: avaritia (greed or covetousness) is the capital vice of excessive attachment to material goods, including insatiable acquisition and hoarding, classically contrasted with liberality and justice.
plainSummary: In this list, greed denotes a disordered love of possessing—holding or seeking wealth in a way that subordinates justice, charity, or the common good.

name: Lust (luxuria) as capital vice
description: Derived principle: luxuria (lust) is the capital vice of inordinate sexual appetite—desire that ignores temperance, consent, covenant, or the integral good of persons, as classically articulated in Christian sexual ethics.
plainSummary: In this tradition, lust denotes sexual desire disordered by object, circumstance, or intent—treating persons as mere means to appetite.

name: Pride (superbia) as capital vice
description: Derived principle from Christian moral tradition: pride (superbia) is a root distortion of self-love—excessive esteem for oneself, contempt for dependence on God or others—often treated as ordering or amplifying other vices.
plainSummary: In the classic list, pride is the disordered elevation of self—elevating the self above God, truth, or the good of others.

name: Sloth (acedia) as capital vice
description: Derived principle: acedia (sloth) is the capital vice of spiritual torpor or sorrow at the demands of the good—classically distinct from clinical depression, though the two raise difficult pastoral and medical questions.
plainSummary: In this list, sloth is not mere laziness: it is spiritual apathy—refusal of the good one owes, especially toward God and neighbor.

name: Wrath (ira) as capital vice
description: Derived principle: ira (wrath or anger as vice) is the capital vice of disordered anger—resentment, rage, or cruelty that seeks harm beyond just defense or proportionate correction; classically distinguished from righteous anger at genuine injustice.
plainSummary: In this list, wrath denotes unjust anger—desire for vengeance or cruelty out of proportion to a real or perceived wrong.

name: Common law method
description: Much of U.S. law (especially in contracts, torts, property, and procedure) develops through judicial decisions that articulate, distinguish, and incrementally reshape rules—alongside statutes and constitutions.

name: Constitutional supremacy
description: The U.S. Constitution is the supreme law of the land; inconsistent statutes and other government acts yield to it (including state law under the Supremacy Clause).

name: Due process of law
description: Due process requires government to follow fair procedures—and in substantive strands, to respect certain baseline protections—before depriving persons of life, liberty, or property (Fifth Amendment as to federal power; Fourteenth as to states).

name: Equal protection of the laws
description: The Equal Protection Clause bars states from denying any person within their jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws; classifications among persons require justification by standards that vary with the context and the right at stake.

name: Federalism (division of sovereign authority)
description: Sovereignty is split between a national government and the states: each has distinct lawmaking and enforcement domains, with federal law supreme only within enumerated federal powers.

name: Judicial review
description: Courts may assess whether statutes and executive actions comply with the Constitution and refuse to enforce those that do not—tying the written constitution to ordinary adjudication.

name: Rule of law
description: Government officials—including law enforcement and courts—are bound by law; powers are exercised through known rules and procedures rather than arbitrary will, supporting predictability and accountability.

name: Separation of powers
description: Legislative, executive, and judicial functions are assigned to distinct branches at the federal level, with checks and balances intended to prevent concentrated power and arbitrary rule.

name: Stare decisis (respect for precedent)
description: Courts generally follow prior decisions on the same legal question to promote stability, reliance, and equal treatment—while allowing rare departures when precedent is unworkable or egregiously wrong.

name: US Right to Try Act
description: Enacted federal law that allows terminally ill patients to access experimental treatments that have completed Phase I clinical trials but are not yet FDA-approved.
